data.title: Without Fear or Favour: An insider's account of judicial power and politics
data.description:
Without Fear or Favour  by Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul with Jay Vinayak Ojha
Published by Juggernaut
340 pages             ₹999
 
To those with only academic knowledge of how India’s higher judiciary functions and its dealings with the government, this book is an unnerving revelation because it confirms, per an insider’s account and not just tittle-tattle at a paan  shop, what was always dismissed as speculation. The author was a member of the Collegium when D Y Chandrachud (now retired) was Chief Justice of India (CJI). That he thought Chandrachud was “too deferential to the Government” could be a personal opinion. But when he says as CJI, Chandrachud sought the government’s “nod” on a candidate to be elevated as a judge to the Supreme Court before the Collegium had met and once even gave voice to its “bizarre” query regarding the caste of a minority-faith judge candidate, the matter goes beyond mere gossip.
 
 
He writes: “On the day, while going to the [Collegium] meeting, Dhan [CJI Chandrachud] proposed a sixth name…. I suspected the name had been proposed at the government’s instance.” There was a dispute among others in the Collegium on the name. The CJI then took him aside and “wondered aloud whether he should telephone out to check the Government’s view”.
 
On the question of appointing a judge from a minority, he writes, the government asked whether more representation was needed, given that judges from other religious minorities were already serving. “I was troubled by this logic,” Kaul writes. The government wanted to know, according to him, what caste the individual had been from before he changed his faith. “The follow-up was chilling: Dhan shared something with me as the government view that I must now redact, but it did provoke me. ‘If this is how we are going to appoint judges,’ I said, ‘you may as well consult and appoint yourself. Chief Justices used to appoint judges before the collegium was created. You may do it that way. I cannot be party to such a decision’,” Kaul writes. He then says he walked out of the meeting.
 
This and accounts of other such incidents are likely to leave readers slack-jawed. The value of this book is precisely this: That it is the narration of an insider. 
 
Asked about these statements, Justice Chandrachud had told The Indian Express: “It is very difficult for me to comment on what Sanjay Kaul has written because I have not read the book. So unless I read what he has written, and in what context he has written it, I cannot give a detailed reaction.” He also said he could not “recall an occasion when Sanjay Kaul walked out of a Collegium meeting”.
 
On dealings with the government, Kaul is realistic. He writes, “It is fantasy to imagine that the Collegium is isolated from political pressures. Governments assert themselves. If you give them an opening, they will grab it. The challenge is to maintain institutional integrity while navigating these pressures. Indeed, I found that the Government has far more respect for judges with a spine in such matters and the need for balance.”
 
He believes judiciary-executive relations unravelled after the National Judicial Appointments Commission legislation, which gave the government a veto in judicial appointments, was struck down by the Supreme Court.
 
Kaul is forthright on other issues that have confused ordinary Indians. How far should judges go in accepting government largesse? He writes he once asked Chief Justice Ranjan Gogoi why he accepted a seat in the Rajya Sabha after his retirement. To this, Gogoi replied that if such a thing is offered, one must not refuse as a matter of duty, Kaul says. “That’s his perspective. Mine is that it’s simply not worth one’s while,” he writes. Of course, one can debate if this extends to judges inviting the men holding the most important jobs in the land to pujas at their residence or a grandson’s mundan ceremony as a CJI and a Supreme Court judge are reported to have done.
 
In the manner of a reporter, Kaul narrates what he calls “an Institutional Earthquake”. In 2018, Justices Jasti Chelameswar, Ranjan Gogoi, Madan Lokur and Kurian Joseph flagged concerns about the functioning of the court and the Chief Justice’s allocation of cases — at a press conference. Kaul’s view is that while the concerns of the judges might have been valid, a press conference was maybe not the route to resolving them. While the incident remains one of the most extraordinary episodes in the Supreme Court’s recent history, taking internal disagreements into the public domain has a cost, he believes.
 
But the book is not only about the independence of the judiciary. It is about everyday justice (Kaul regrets he wasn’t able to do enough to reduce delays and pendency) and running the administrative system that dispenses justice. 
 
The account of his handling of pugilistic lawyers in the Madras High Court, where he was appointed Chief Justice, is a must-read for students of management. Equally interesting is his description of a fellow High Court judge, Justice C S Karnan, who passed away on November 13, 2026. While he was alive, he had beef with everybody. He was the first sitting High Court judge to be sentenced to six months in prison for contempt of court — and he was a part of Justice Kaul’s life in Chennai. (He was arrested and jailed after retirement.) 
 
Kaul also writes about his tenure in the Punjab and Haryana High Court as Chief Justice, which was short but nurturing.

data.title: Unicorns on the beach: Goa bets big on startups, but can size be a hurdle?
data.description:
When childhood friends Rohin Parkar and Malcom D’Souza decided to start a venture in their native state of Goa, the techies had one thought in mind. “Keys are going to go away,” Parkar recalls — an allusion to the fact that the physical keys to a home will give way to a world of digital and wireless access.
 
The government of Goa is taking the thought a step further — it’s promoting the tourism haven as a place where seamless digital living will be a natural home to India’s army of startup dreamers.
 
It’s easy to see why. Goa’s golden beaches, fume-free air and blue skies helped unleash the creative tech juices for the childhood buddies. That single potent metaphor-friendly thought — a keyless home — led to the creation of Spintly, a successful Goan startup. It provides smart, contactless management and security for buildings. Having raised $10 million so far, Spintly has a clientele ranging from Godrej and Tata Consumer Products to Anarock and JLL. 
 
“Starting Spintly in Goa was never a compromise; it was a choice. In the end it was persistence and patience that paid,” Parkar said.
 
The coastal state has also produced India’s first medtech company, Molbio Diagnostics. Started by Sriram Natarajan in 2000, it has gone on to develop the world’s only commercial field-usable battery-operated PCR (polymerase chain reaction) platform, which can help in the quick detection of viruses, bacteria, parasites and fungi.  
 
Not surprisingly, both companies played an important role during the Covid pandemic, amid a need for minimising physical contact and increasing real-time testing. 
 
Post-Covid success
 
Today, sun-kissed beaches, laid-back living and a thriving party scene are not all that Goa is known for. With many Indians turning up, looking for a remote working spot, the number of startups has also seen a sharp increase. 
 
The number of startups in 2020, towards the end of the pandemic was a mere 132. As of September 2026, there were 846 of them, according to government data. In the last two years alone, 100-150 startups have moved to Goa from cities that are strongly associated with the startup boom — Delhi NCR, Mumbai and Bengaluru.
 
To be sure, Goa is not likely to rival Bengaluru, Mumbai or Gurgaon anytime soon in the number of startups or the depth of their venture-capital networks. But the coastal state is building its pitch on a different proposition: A place where founders can live better, drift into blue-sky thinking and build new age companies in tech, artificial intelligence (AI) and design. 
 
The modest size of the state and its small population, most of whom are fluent in English, are factors the government hopes will entice interested entrepreneurs. Government officials say several entrepreneurs have already made Goa their second home — or a place to start their second or third venture. 
 
“Infrastructure-wise Goa has become a lot more sorted. It has become a lot easier and doable to start a company from here…The brain works better here,” said Radhika Ghai, founder of ecommerce startups such as ShopClues and Kindlife. Ghai advises Goa’s startup division and though her company is based in Delhi, all her work around strategy and planning gets done in Goa. 
 
“My team works from Goa four or five times a year. We are considering opening an office here,” Ghai added. 
 
While Ghai may be a visitor with a second home in Goa, founder Kartikeya Tiwari moved his business to the coastal state from Delhi to start his second venture.
 
Tiwari first came to Goa in 2016 with a technology app for hotels. The idea, he says, came from the late Chief Minister  Manohar Parrikar who was clear that there could be no better place than Goa to try out any hotel-related product in India. 
 
Tiwari stayed on to cofound GoBro, which claims to be India’s first AI-powered “super property app” that consolidates the real estate ecosystem into a single unified platform. Tiwari is taking GoBro to Pune and Mumbai. 
 
Ten years on, Tiwari is still there. “What works for Goa is its smallness, its very piloting nature.  The distances are shorter and the total population is less, which makes the response time much better,” Tiwari said. 
 
There’s something else that has kept him moored in Goa: “You don’t lose a thought, an idea can live with you for a longer time. That is very entrepreneur-friendly.”
 
Work from home? Try a beach
 
The state has come a long way from where it was ten years ago, when it was a struggle for people like Ghai to find a spot with good wifi to do an online meeting. The availability of high-speed internet has improved, with connectivity now available in remote villages as well. Road links, too, have been ramped up over the years.
 
A shackathon organised in May this year saw many founders, professionals, “digital nomads” come down to explore working from the beaches. 
 
“Shacks are already there. All we need to do is ensure that the basic amenities like high speed internet connectivity are available,” Rohan Khaunte, tourism and IT minister of Goa said. 
 
“We’re talking about providing pods like those in airports. Digital nomads were already present in Goa but not at the beach. We are now giving them a spread. We are saying work from the beach.” 
 
All of this has been part of Goa’s quiet attempt to look beyond tourism — cleverly using its existing tourist infrastructure to build a knowledge economy. Tourism and hospitality account for 16 per cent of the gross state domestic product. Services as a whole contributes 47 per cent, according to the FY2024-25 Economic Survey of the state. 
 
The potential is real. IT has the most number of registered startups in Goa with 96, followed by food and beverages (86) with several popular brands of gin, coffee having started here. Travel and tourism, and healthcare and lifesciences are other two major areas. 
 
The size question
 
But Goa’s smallness is also a constraint. 
 
Parkar had to step out of Goa to raise funds for Spindly, pointing to the absence of an investor ecosystem. Tiwari, too, is planning to visit Dubai soon to raise funds for GoBro. “There is no major investor community in Goa. I got a lot of funding through friends and family. A lot of institutional money came through the US,” Parkar said. 
 
Private equity and venture capital firms however, are smelling an opportunity in Goa, especially for niche startups. “Entrepreunerships in metros is fairly choked. Goa has emerged as a very strong platform for founders. The quality of thinking is tremendously high. A number of VCs (venture capital funds) are setting shop in Goa as well. VCs are agnostic where you come from,” said Siddharth Pai, founding partner at 3One4 Capital, a Bengaluru-based early-stage venture capital firm.
 
“Goa can create a niche of startups with fewer people and bigger wallet sizes. Goa cannot handle volume – it has to embrace a knowledge-based small team ethos.”   
 
Accessing talent, especially for positions at higher levels, has also been a challenge for many entrepreneurs. While D S Prashant, chief executive officer at Goa’s startup promotion cell, cited the example of a startup founder who was able to hire a CEO in Goa for a much smaller salary than what he would pay in a metro city, founders said that there is a talent-opportunity mismatch.
 
“Many are leaving Goa to find talent. The government can play a role in getting incubators. Colleges need to become a part of this process. Students are not starting companies in Goa,” Parkar said.
 
Tiwari added, “Team leads are coming from other cities. Freshers and mid-level students come from Goa.” 
 
The gameplan
 
Goa’s startup promotion cell had set a target of spawning 1,000 startups by 2027, but seeing the milestone already within reach well ahead of the deadline, the state feels that it is not the numbers alone they should be chasing — quality’s needed, too.
 
“Out of these 1,000 we want at least 10 to become really big. That is when we will see a big transformation. In the next five years we want Goa to have a few $1 billion companies,” said Prashant. 
 
Molbio Diagnostics, India’s first medtech unicorn which attained a valuation of $1.6 billion in 2022 after raising $85 million from Singapore-based Temasek and existing investor Motilal Oswal Alternates, shows that it can be done. 
 
While a better environment, and work-life balance have played a big role in attracting entrepreneurs to start their ventures in Goa, the government is conscious that these alone do not spell a sustainable strategy. 
 
“We need some pull factor. We are making it liberal for anyone to be able to come. The government is becoming a user of technology…We have to set up a fund of funds. The government has not put in its money yet and so there will be some skin in the game for us,” Prashant added. 
 
The state is planning to start an exercise to map the skillset of people in Goa and then match it with the needs of startup founders. Thereafter, it wants to plug the gaps by providing training wherever required. 
 
The startup cell is also trying to woo investors to Goa, as well as create its own investment fund as part of a recently unveiled AI policy.
 
With an outlay of ₹250 crore for three years starting FY27, Goa has joined a growing group of states such as Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Odisha that have drawn up dedicated AI policies. 
 
Goa’s policy seeks to provide up to 600 micro, small and medium businesses free AI-readiness assessment, subsidised advisory, mentoring, Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) compliance guidance and implementation subsidies.  The policy promises fast-track registration with a single window for approval within 30 days.
 
The state government also plans to roll out AI training in schools from academic year 2027-28 and open AI labs in up to 50 government-run schools.
 
Deepak Pathania, founder-member of the Creative Community of Goa, an organisation that works with the state government to help shape Goa’s design policy and grow its creative ecosystem, said he wants to make the state a destination for design and creative businesses.
 
“Creative work thrives in environments that offer inspiration, flexibility and room to explore, and Goa has long attracted people seeking that way of life…This makes Goa an attractive and cost-effective location for companies to establish design offices here,” Pathania said.

data.title: Irdai fines Star Health ₹2 crore over unjustified health claim rejections
data.description:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) on Thursday said it had imposed a penalty of ₹2 crore on Star Health and Allied Insurance for repudiating health insurance claims on untenable grounds and making deductions not supported by policy terms, including in cases involving Covid-19 claims.
 
The order was based on an inspection conducted between January 31 and February 11, 2022.
 
Irdai found that in several sampled cases, claims were paid only after it flagged the discrepancies. It also noted that policyholders were not informed of the specific policy provisions under which their claims were rejected or deductions made, limiting their ability to challenge the decisions.
 
 
The penalty comprises ₹1 crore for violations relating to claim repudiations and ₹1 crore for unsupported deductions and inadequate communication of claim decisions.
 
The insurer was also warned over discounts agreed with network hospitals not being reflected in bills or disclosed to policyholders. Irdai directed Star Health to itemise allowed, disallowed, non-payable and discount amounts, along with reductions in the sum insured, in claim settlement letters.
 
The insurer has been directed to place the order before its board and submit an action-taken report.

data.title: Oil prices set for 3rd straight week of decline on West Asia export flows
data.description:
Oil prices fell on Friday and were set for a weekly decline ??on strong exports from West Asia despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
 Brent crude futures were down 53 cents, or 0.6 per cent, at $91.45 a barrel at 1145 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures for December were down 81 cents, or 1 per cent, at $82.40 a barrel, while the more active January contract was down 24 cents, or 0.3 per cent, at $82.20.
 Brent is on track for a 5 per cent decline for the week and the December WTI contract for a 7 per cent weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. This would be the benchmarks' third straight week of decline.
 
 “This week we keep having relatively strong export flows out of West Asia. There is also a narrative ongoing that as long as people are talking, maybe there's a deal in the making,” said Aldo Spanjer, commodity strategist at BNP Paribas.   

Gold slides toward worst week in 8 mths on hawkish Fed outlook

 Gold fell for a fifth day — heading for the biggest weekly decline since March — as a hawkish Federal Reserve signaled more interest-rate hikes and a rout in AI stocks spurred selling across metals markets. Bullion tumbled to trade near $3,500 an ounce on Friday, and was on track to lose about 8 per cent this week, after hitting its lowest level since September 2025. Silver has fallen almost 15 per cent over the past five sessions. This rout marks a decisive capitulation below $4,000 an ounce, a level some investors believed would provide a floor for bullion, supported by central-bank purchases and other dip-buyers.The severity of gold's slide has been difficult to attribute to any visible seller. Bullion holdings in popular exchange-traded funds have mostly risen since the summer, while speculators on the Comex futures exchange have not aggressively shed bullish positions. A chorus of Fed officials signaling further interest rate hikes has continued to weigh on gold, which generally suffers when borrowing costs rise as it doesn’t pay interest.   

Mahanadi IPO booked 48% on Day 2

 The initial public offering (IPO) of Mahanadi Coalfields, a subsidiary of state-owned Coal India, received 48 per cent subscription on the second day of bidding on Friday. The category for Qualified Institutional Buyers was subscribed 1.37 times, while the retail quota was booked 24 per cent. The non-institutional investors' segment was subscribed 18 per cent. The IPO price band has been fixed at ₹129-136 per share, valuing the company at a little over ₹90,000 crore. The issue will close on November 23.  

Crystal Crop  IPO booked 17x on final day

 The initial public offering (IPO) of Crystal Crop Protection was subscribed 17 times on the final day of bidding on Friday. The category for non-institutional investors was subscribed 37.70 times, while the portion for qualified institutional buyers received 15.47 times subscription. The quota for retail investors was subscribed 9.28 times. The IPO of Crystal Crop Protection  was fully booked on the first day of bidding on Wednesday. The price band was fixed at ₹ 259-272 per share, with a valuation of ₹4,438 crore at the upper end.

data.title: Wife brand vs Mistress Brand: Can public status outweigh private utility?
data.description:
There are two kinds of brands in our lives. The Wife Brand and The Mistress Brand.
 
The Wife Brand is the one you marry. You show her off. You introduce her to your parents, to your boss, to society. She has pedigree. She is expensive. She looks good in photos. You bought her after a lot of research and after taking a loan.
 
The Mistress Brand is the one you actually love spending time with. She is comfortable. She is fun. She doesn’t judge you. She is there for you every day, at home, when no one is watching. You didn’t take out a loan for her. You just picked her up because she made you feel good.
 
One is for log kya kahenge (what will people say?). The other is for mujhe kya chahiye (what do I want?).
 
Ask a man in Gurugram what watch he wears. He will say, “Rolex.” That’s his Wife Brand. Now ask him what watch he wears when he goes for a morning walk. It is a G-Shock. Or an Apple Watch. That is his Mistress Brand.
 
The Wife Brand is for the boardroom. The Mistress Brand is for the bedroom.
 
Women do it too. Every woman has a Wife Brand handbag — Louis Vuitton, never out of its dust bag, used only for weddings and kitty outings. And a Mistress Brand handbag — Zara tote, or that big Fabindia jhola that goes everywhere. She loves the jhola. She respects the LV.
 
This is the most powerful, most unspoken truth of Indian consumer behaviour. And most brands never understand it. We are a country of two-brand lives.
 
We buy an Apple iPhone — that's the Wife. We flaunt it on Instagram. But our second phone, the one with two SIMs and a big battery for the driver and the house help to call, is a OnePlus or a Xiaomi. That’s the Mistress. Nearly 70 per cent of iPhone users in India also own an Android. Apple will never tell you this.
 
We buy Nike shoes — Wife Brand. ~12,000. For the gym photos. But for the daily 5 km walk in the park? Skechers. Or Bata. Comfortable, soft, no one will judge. Nike is for society. Skechers is for the soul. That’s why Skechers sells more pairs in India than Nike, even though Nike spends 10 times more on advertising.
 
We even eat this way.
 
Olive oil is the Wife Brand. We keep the bottle in front of the kitchen so guests can see. We use it when the nutritionist comes. But the daily tadka? Fortune refined oil. Or desi ghee. The Mistress Brand that actually makes the food taste good. Olive oil is respect. Ghee is love.
 
Why does the Wife exist then? Because India is still a status society. We don’t buy brands only for ourselves. We buy brands for our neighbours, our relatives, our office colleagues.
 
A Rolex doesn’t tell time better. It tells people your time has come. A Mercedes doesn’t drive better in Gurugram traffic. It tells people you have arrived, even if you haven't moved 100 meters in 30 minutes.
 
Wife Brands are signal brands. They signal success, taste, arrival. But Mistress Brands are utility brands. They work. They are loyal.
 
And here is the marketing secret no one tells you: Wife Brands make the noise. Mistress Brands make the money.
 
So what should a brand want to be? Being a Wife Brand is expensive. You have to spend all the time to stay beautiful. You have to do ads with Alia Bhatt. You have to be on the cover of Vogue.
 
Mistress Brands are resilient. No one cares if Skechers didn’t do an ad with Ranveer. No one trolls Bata.
 
The smartest brands in the last 10 years chose to be Mistresses, not Wives.
 
Look at Zudio. Zudio never said, “We are premium.” Zudio said, “We are your daily wear.” It is the ultimate Mistress Brand to Zara’s Wife Brand. Zara is where you go to impress. Zudio is where you go to live. Today Zudio sells more than Zara and H&M combined.
 
If you are a Wife Brand, accept it. Spend money. Stay beautiful. Be ready for judgement. And know that you will be loved in public, but maybe not used every day.
 
If you are a Mistress Brand, stop trying to become the Wife. Stop doing luxury ads. Stop hiring that expensive agency. Embrace your role. Be comfortable. Be available. Be affordable. Be there at 11 pm when they need you.
 
People stay for the Wife.
 
But they live for the Mistress.
 
The writer is chairman, Rediffusion

data.title: PM Balendra Shah's brief Delhi visit unfolds amid Nepal's domestic strains
data.description:
When Nepal Prime Minister (PM) Balendra Shah (36) arrives in India on November 22 on his first state visit, it will be the briefest bilateral sojourn in New Delhi by any PM from that country: He leaves on November 23, without taking up the government’s offer of showing him around Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Ayodhya, or Varanasi.
 
But for the 25 hours he is in New Delhi, Mr Shah will leave domestic worries behind. He took office eight months ago, on the back of the stupendous electoral victory of the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), popularised by its election symbol, the ghanti (bell). From 11 seats in the last general election, the RSP shot up to 182 in a 275-member house in the 2026 poll, just two short of a two-thirds majority. The irony is that even with this order of seats, the government is hobbled: Zero seats in the Upper House or in any of the provinces. The next set of elections to the Upper House is scheduled for 2028. So, till then, only those reforms on which there is a political consensus are likely to become law. By temperament, Mr Shah is not a consensus man, nor is diplomacy his forte. This makes structural reform via legislation a bit harder. To make up for this, the government has tended to resort to optics to showcase its work: The arrest of former Prime Minister K P Sharma Oli and former home minister Ramesh Lekhak, for instance, or the attempted arrest of Nepali Congress leader and former Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba on charges of money laundering, nixed because of legal infirmities.
 
This could be because Mr Shah’s Cabinet is the youngest in Nepal’s history and only two of its 17 members have ministerial experience. Expectations are high, but promises made during the campaign are nowhere near fulfilment. The most consequential among them is land reform, specifically land ownership certificates, called Lalpurja (because of the red paper on which they are printed). Like in India, not all tillers of land are certified owners. They may have owned the land for generations but without a valid, verified Lalpurja. There’s simply no legally recognised property ownership in Nepal. Banks won’t approve loans against unverified land. Government offices won’t process transfers. Courts won’t uphold ownership claims without it. This is one reason for the infancy of Nepal’s real-estate sector. But there is also politics. Lalpurja was a signal promise of the RSP during the elections. But given his background as mayor of Kathmandu and his ruthless action against squatters and encroachment, Mr Shah has indeed ordered clearing squatters but has paid scant attention to how these families should be re-housed. If this is ignored (many so-called squatter families are currently housed in camps) the mood could turn against the ghanti very quickly.
 
Corruption is another serious problem. Tiny Lame Ahal village, just outside Pokhara, one of Nepal’s biggest tourist destinations, used to be conservative and determinedly pro-Nepali Congress. At 50-something, Ganga Gurung is not a typical ghanti supporter. Ghanti supporters tend to be younger. But she says dramatically: “Even if you hold a pistol to my head, I will vote Ghanti. They opened our eyes.” Although party chief Rabi Lamichhane has cases of corruption against him (he was in prison when “liberated” by a mob that led to Mr Oli’s resignation), there is no movement on those files. Scandals involving “fixers” and the rigging of courts abound.
 
Existential problems continue. Lack of employment has been exacerbated by the return of migrant workers from West Asia. In March this year alone, of the three million who work in the region, around 6,000 Nepali workers had applied online to return home. The remittances these migrants sent back to Nepal represent more than a third of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) and some of them could now need to find employment at home. Natural disasters have added another dimension to the management of emergencies in Nepal.
 
That foreign policy is not a priority for the Shah government is understandable though appearing to balance the interests of India and China in the region is crucial if Nepal wants to be left in peace. When he comes to India, the two sides are likely to unveil a 10-year vision document: A peek at this reveals nothing new. The two most contentious areas — India’s Agniveer scheme and the recruitment challenge it represents for Nepal; and differences on the delineation of the border — are unlikely to come any closer to resolution during this trip. Nepal’s attention is also divided: When the PM is in India, a large high-ranking parliamentary delegation will be in China at the invitation of the Chinese Communist Party at the same time. Although China has been courting Nepal with its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), financing for it is yet to come.
 
The unknown element is the role of the United States (US) in Nepal. In the past, US policy used to be influenced by India’s stance. This is gradually changing, though Kathmandu is wary of riling New Delhi on this score.
 
For Mr Shah, being different is crucial. The outcome to look out for is whether New Delhi acknowledges this.

data.title: Supreme Court pulls up Registry over ED appeal pending for nearly 3 years
data.description:
The Supreme Court on Friday sought an explanation from its Registry for failing to list an Enforcement Directorate (ED) appeal for nearly three years, despite repeated directions to take up the matter.
 
A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, expressed displeasure over the delay in listing the appeal challenging anticipatory bail granted to businessman Raman Singhal in a money laundering case.
 
“Why has this matter not been listed? September 2023, September 2024, September 2025, September 2026. This is what I want to know,” the CJI asked.
 
When a lawyer suggested that the delay could have been due to the non-availability of Benches, the CJI responded, “All Benches are available.”
 
 
Justice Bagchi described the lapse as “nothing but institutional lethargy”.
 
The CJI subsequently directed the Registry to explain why the matter had not been listed despite earlier judicial directions. However, the court declined to entertain the ED's appeal, observing that the trial had progressed substantially.
 
The appeal arose from a January 30, 2023, order of the Punjab and Haryana High Court granting anticipatory bail to Singhal in a case involving an alleged bank fraud of ₹155.21 crore.
 
The ED alleged that Mahesh Timbers Private Limited had fraudulently enhanced Foreign Letters of Credit (FLCs) and diverted the funds obtained through these transactions to Amazon Exports Pte Limited, a Singapore-based company in which Singhal was a director.
 
According to the agency, the transactions resulted in a loss of ₹155.21 crore to the bank. Singhal was named as one of the accused in the money laundering investigation.
 
While granting him anticipatory bail, the high court had taken note of the fact that the ED had already filed its prosecution complaint. It also observed that Singhal could not be arrested at that stage without a warrant from the trial court.
 
The ED challenged the high court's decision before the Supreme Court in May 2023. The apex court issued notice in September 2023 and subsequently passed several directions for relisting the matter, including orders for its listing for final hearing or disposal.
 
Despite these directions, the appeal remained pending without an effective hearing for almost three years.
 
Senior Advocate Siddharth Dave, appearing for Singhal, expressed surprise at the delay, saying he had been practising in the Supreme Court since 1990 and had rarely encountered such a situation.
 
Senior Advocate Zoheb Hossain, appearing for the ED, suggested that the delay could be because Dave was not in the Supreme Court Registry.
 
“Don't quibble with me about all these things. I am only saying these things don't happen,” Dave responded.
 
The Bench was also informed that the trial had commenced and eight witnesses had already been examined. Taking note of the progress in the trial, the court declined to entertain the ED's appeal and disposed of the petition.
 
However, it clarified that the order granting anticipatory bail would neither be treated as a precedent nor influence the outcome of the trial.
 
“The impugned (challenged) order shall neither be treated as a precedent nor shall have any impact on the outcome of the trial,” the court said.

data.title: Anthropic shares tumble after record IPO as AI trade faces reality check
data.description:
Anthropic's much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Friday, as a dramatic unravelling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.
 
Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic's listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing after a turbulent stretch.
 
But the stock was last trading at $88.24, about 9 per cent below Thursday's close, while losses across other technology heavyweights suggested the IPO had done little to reverse the broader selloff.
 
"Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth," said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds.
 
 
Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia and Meta Platforms fell more than 3 per cent each, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped 2 per cent and 1 per cent, respectively.
 
Chip stocks also slid, with AMD and Sandisk down over 6 per cent each and Intel losing more than 3 per cent.
 
The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which would be another major test of investors' appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year.
 
Despite a pipeline of high-profile AI and infrastructure companies, many have pushed their IPO plans to 2027.
 
PATIENCE MAY PAY
 
Anthropic's stock could find support later in the year. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 per cent of Anthropic's shares by year-end.
 
Near-term volatility, however, could persist as the initial euphoria around the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.
 
"We favour patience on Anthropic and recommend evaluating the company as it reports public results," said Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, adding that the current valuation "assumes years of rapid growth."
 
The debut has also done little to ease broader concerns about the health of the AI trade. Wall Street's main indices ended sharply lower on Thursday, while futures pointed to further declines on Friday.
 
PARALLELS WITH SPACEX
 
Anthropic's IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which went public in June after the second-biggest IPO on record.
 
Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in its IPO after underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares, surpassing SpaceX's $85.7 billion haul to become the biggest listing on record.
 
While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX's sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing.
 
"There's going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don't think there's any need to get on it on the first trade," said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co.
 
SpaceX shares fell more than 6 per cent.
 
Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012.
 
The stock's sharp swings have left investors weighing whether to bet on a rebound or brace for further losses. Options trading, due to begin next week, could add to the volatility.
 
"It's not a good environment for Anthropic at the moment," said Carsten Hesse, head of index events at Berenberg.

data.title: Labour unions push for higher wages, job guarantees in FY28 Budget talks
data.description:
Labour-sector stakeholders sought higher minimum wages, wider social security coverage, stronger employment guarantees and measures to address youth unemployment at a pre-Budget consultation chaired by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Friday, according to people aware of the matter.
 
Other proposals included lower goods and services tax (GST) on staffing services, gig worker protections and higher pensions.
 
The Indian Staffing Federation (ISF) proposed cutting GST on staffing and manpower supply services from 18 per cent to 5 per cent, while retaining full input tax credit. It said the current rate raised formal hiring costs by around 13 percentage points, making it less competitive against informal and gig arrangements. The proposed cut could generate 15-20 million additional formal jobs over the medium term, including 1.5-2 million in the near term. The gross tax differential was estimated at ₹28,000 crore, with a lower actual revenue impact after input tax credits.
 
ISF also sought a one-time ₹7,000 employer incentive for hiring skilled youngsters for first formal jobs, subject to verified EPF enrolment and retention. It proposed extending the PM Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana by two years until July 2029, opening the PM Internship Scheme to companies with annual turnover of at least ₹100 crore and linking stipend support to formal job conversion. Other demands included a national skilling-to-employment mission focused on placements rather than enrolments and allowing corporate social responsibility funds to finance hostels for migrant and women workers near industrial clusters.
 
Communist Party of India (Marxist) CPI (M)-affiliated Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU) demanded a national minimum wage of ₹42,000 per month, a publicly funded minimum income guarantee of the same amount for those outside regular wage employment and a universal monthly pension of ₹21,000 for the elderly. It also sought restoration of the Old Pension Scheme, repeal of the four Labour Codes and 200 days of employment under the rural employment guarantee scheme, alongside an urban employment guarantee. It criticised the ₹30,000-crore allocation under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme head for 2026-27, against ₹88,000 crore in the previous year’s revised estimates.
 
CITU further called for filling vacancies in government departments, semi-government establishments and public-sector undertakings, and time-bound regularisation of eligible contractual workers. Its other demands included a legal guarantee for minimum support prices, stronger public procurement, universal public distribution, health care spending at 3 per cent of the gross domestic product (GDP) and education spending at 6 per cent. It also sought protection against job displacement due to artificial intelligence and automation, wealth and inheritance taxes, and higher taxation of extraordinary corporate profits.
 
The Trade Union Co-ordination Centre (TUCC) sought monthly minimum honorariums of ₹10,000 for Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) workers, ₹15,000 for Anganwadi workers and ₹12,000 for helpers, along with EPF coverage. It also called for EPFO and ESIC benefits for construction workers, funded through state building and other construction workers’ welfare cess funds, and appointment letters, minimum wages and social security for contractual railway goods shed workers. Eligible workers above 60 should receive gratuity and terminal benefits, it said.
 
TUCC proposed doubling the gratuity ceiling from ₹20 lakh to ₹40 lakh and raising the calculation from 15 to 21 days’ wages for every completed year of service. It also sought welfare boards for fishermen, street vendors and transport workers, and subsidised EPF and ESIC contributions for eligible micro, small and medium enterprises, with the Centre and states sharing costs equally. Other demands included free family health insurance for lower-income households whose members had paid income tax for five consecutive years.
 
For gig workers, TUCC proposed an aggregator-funded social security fund, health insurance of up to ₹5 lakh and comprehensive accident cover, with registration through e-Shram.
 
The Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS) also flagged youth unemployment and vacancies in state governments and public-sector undertakings, where many workers were employed on contract. It sought a proposal to fill these posts and a National Wage Policy providing for regular minimum wage revisions in line with inflation and the cost of living, with periodic tripartite reviews. It also proposed raising the income-tax threshold from ₹12 lakh to ₹20 lakh.
 
The Telangana Gig and Platform Workers’ Union and the Indian Federation of App-Based Transport Workers sought a dedicated gig worker welfare board, backed by budgetary support and fixed platform contributions for every completed transaction. Citing unpredictable earnings, unsafe conditions, arbitrary rate changes and sudden account blocking, they called for fair payments, transparent platform reporting, safeguards against arbitrary termination and effective grievance redressal. They also flagged opaque algorithm-based management and limited collective bargaining rights, seeking health and accident insurance and pension benefits.

data.title: India must rethink aviation strategy to make airlines commercially viable
data.description:
Someone once noted that India has low-fare airlines, not low-cost ones. This is because the cost structures unique to domestic airlines relate to inflexible ones like high fuel prices and taxes, aircraft leasing charges, and high landing and parking charges at major airports.
 
You can run a low-cost airline only if you have special cost advantages, which practically no domestic airline has. Indigo, at some point, seemed to have cracked the code for ensuring high efficiency on relatively low fares, but today — despite having two-thirds of the Indian aviation market and without any real airfare constraints — it is reporting losses.
 
While the quarterly losses are directly related to the two wars that have pushed up fuel costs for everyone, the point is this: If even a near-monopoly airline keeps making losses the minute some cost factor turns unfavourable, where is the case for expanding Indian aviation phenomenally? And Air India, nearly five years after privatisation, is nowhere near breaking even.
 
Consider a few facts. One, despite a massive surge in the creation of new airports, including under the UDAN scheme, some reports note that around 15 airports are either non-functional or unviable, given current traffic levels. With land pricey, and security costs only growing in a world full of challenges from non-state terrorist actors, overall airport costs are only going to rise.  This means airport costs for airlines will not come down anytime soon.
 
Two, low-cost airlines need low-cost infrastructure and much lower fuel prices, but that is not going to happen in India when both Centre and states rely heavily on revenues from fuel taxation to meet budgetary needs.
 
Three, the main factor supporting the growth of aviation is speed of travel between two cities. But most cities do not have the necessary connectivity from city to airports, making the actual cost and time taken to travel much greater than what the headline says. The waiting time for passengers at most airports is also very high, given delays and security needs.
 
Four, the rapid expansion of high-speed rail, possibly over the next 10 years, will make short-distance air travel a less enticing option. Railways Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has gone on record to say that 99 per cent of short-distance travel will be done by rail, and airlines had better watch out.
 
Five, far-flung places like the Northeast will still require airline services, but these cannot happen without large and repeated state subsidies. Defence needs will also necessitate heavy subsidies for airports in these regions.
 
India needs to rethink its airline and airports strategy so that it starts making commercial and social sense. The question: Why do we keep investing so much in a sector that, with the smallest of disruptions, seems likely to go into losses and in need of government support? The International Air Transport Association sees the global airline industry’s net profit margin dropping by half to 2 per cent in 2026, thanks to the various disruptions. And even this gross margin figure hides the real state of the industry. Most airlines are probably under water.
 
This is not to suggest that India should not be investing in aviation, but it must rethink how it can do so smartly. When gestation periods are so high, why should we be investing in a sector with such low returns?
 
So what do we need to rethink?
 
First, we should not allow any new airport to come up without actually building the infrastructure and connectivity for it. This goes not only for small airports in the hinterland, but also for airports in high-density routes. Consider how long it takes to travel from Bengaluru’s software hub in Electronics City to the new airport. One has to add at least two hours each way for the journey to the airport, and a further hour at the landing end. This is more than the time spent in the air.
 
Consider also the extreme reluctance of airlines to shift from Terminal 1 in Mumbai (which is to be rebuilt) to Navi Mumbai. Poor connectivity is possibly the only reason despite the fact that the new airport offers better facilities than the old terminal in Santacruz/Vile Parle.
 
Two, there is a need to liberalise policy to allow domestic ones to fly more abroad, since there is little chance of fuel costs being cut for operations within India. The five-year domestic operation norm before getting permission to fly abroad has been abandoned, but airlines must operate at least 20 aircrafts on domestic routes to fly abroad. Why is this rider needed when most airlines believe that international routes offer them a better yield per passenger, given the opportunity to buy fuel at lower costs abroad?
 
Assuming our overall people and other non-fuel costs are lower than what is the norm globally, won’t Indian airlines benefit from flying more between third countries? This may mean negotiating seventh freedom rights (which allow airlines to operate between any two countries without having a home connection) for Indian airlines, which would also imply allowing airlines based abroad to operate between India and other destinations. What we could do is to allow this only if foreign airlines fly to underutilised large airports like Noida or Navi Mumbai and make them alternative hubs.
 
Three, we need stripped down airports with very low costs (just a runway, one coffee shop and security) in order to allow real low-cost airlines to emerge at some point. The existing rule, which does not allow a greenfield airport to be set up within a 150-km radius of an existing civilian airport, makes this unlikely, though exceptions have been made. The logical thing to do is to negotiate lower revenue shares from airport operators on high-density private airports like Delhi in order to get them to give greater concessions on their monopoly rights. Given the extraordinary amount of time needed to travel to the airport through congested roads, we need more airports closer to city centres. Bengaluru’s software hub would be better served with a basic airport near Hosur in Tamil Nadu than by building another one far away from the city in a completely different direction.
 
Net-net: Many operators entered the airline business looking at it as a trophy business (Vijay Mallya, for example), when in reality it is an albatross for those without deep pockets and patient capital. It is time to change the rules of the game and the policy framework underpinning it. The space must be opened up for competition, while, at the same time, safeguarding the interests of established domestic players.
 
The writer is a senior journalist
